code: CUSTOM_DIFFEXP <- function(se, ri, ci, assay="logcounts") {     ri <- ri$active     if (is.null(ri)) {          ri <- rownames(se)     }     assayMatrix <- assay(se, assay)[ri, , drop=FALSE]      if (is.null(ci$active) || length(ci)<2L) {         return(data.frame(row.names=character(0), LogFC=integer(0))) # dummy value.     }     active <- rowMeans(assayMatrix[,ci$active,drop=FALSE])      all_saved <- ci[grep("saved", names(ci))]     lfcs <- vector("list", length(all_saved))     for (i in seq_along(lfcs)) {         saved <- rowMeans(assayMatrix[,all_saved[[i]],drop=FALSE])         lfcs[[i]] <- active - saved     }      names(lfcs) <- sprintf("LogFC/%i", seq_along(lfcs))     do.call(data.frame, lfcs) } CUSTOM_HEAT <- function(se, ri, ci, assay="logcounts") {     everything <- CUSTOM_DIFFEXP(se, ri, ci, assay=assay)     if (nrow(everything) == 0L) {         return(ggplot()) # empty ggplot if no genes reported.     }      everything <- as.matrix(everything)     top <- head(order(rowMeans(abs(everything)), decreasing=TRUE), 50)     topFC <- everything[top, , drop=FALSE]     dfFC <- data.frame(         gene=rep(rownames(topFC), ncol(topFC)),         contrast=rep(colnames(topFC), each=nrow(topFC)),         value=as.vector(topFC)     )     ggplot(dfFC, aes(contrast, gene)) + geom_raster(aes(fill = value)) } TAB_GEN <- createCustomTable(CUSTOM_DIFFEXP) HEAT_GEN <- createCustomPlot(CUSTOM_HEAT)  rdp[["SelectionHistory"]] <- list(     list(lasso = NULL, closed = TRUE, panelvar1 = NULL, panelvar2 = NULL,          mapping = list(x = "X", y = "Y"),          coord = structure(c(-44.3, -23.7, -13.5, -19.6,             -33.8, -48.6, -44.3, -33.9, -55.4, -43.0,             -19.5, -4.0, -22.6, -33.9), .Dim = c(7L, 2L)         )     ) )  app <- iSEE(sce, initial=list(rdp,     TAB_GEN(ColumnSelectionSource="ReducedDimensionPlot1"),     HEAT_GEN(ColumnSelectionSource="ReducedDimensionPlot1")) )

tour for iSEE - the Interactive SummarizedExperiment Explorer.

You will be shown around the different components of iSEE and learn the basic usage mechanisms by doing. Highlighted elements will respond to the user's actions, while the rest of the UI will be shaded. You will be prompted at particular spots to perform some actions, which will be marked with "Action:" text. Please take care to follow these instructions, since later parts of the tour may assume that all the actions from previous steps have been performed.

Action: now, click on the 'Next' button or use the right arrow of your keyboard to proceed into your tour. #> 2 iSEE provides a Shiny interface that allows you to generate a series of panels for exploring SummarizedExperiment objects. Here, we use single-cell RNA sequencing data from the scRNAseq package, specifically a subset of gene expression profiles from cells in the mouse visual cortex (Tasic et al., 2016). Each column of the SummarizedExperiment corresponds to a cell, while each row corresponds to a gene.

Using iSEE, you can generate a variety of different panel types to visualize the data. These are described in more detail in the following steps. #> 3 For example, you can construct a Reduced dimension plot to visualize a low-dimensional representation (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) of our dataset of interest. Here, each point represents a cell. #> 4 For each plot panel, a variety of parameters are available to control the appearance and behaviour of the plot. These parameters are located in these collapsible boxes, such as the Data parameters box that contains parameters related to the type of data being shown.

Action: click on the header of this collapsible box to see the available options. #> 5 Action: change this to TSNE to see the two-dimensional t-SNE representation. #> 6 You can see how the panel immediately switched to the requested dimensionality reduction result. #> 7 The Visual parameters box contains parameters related to coloring, point appearance, and other visual aspects.

Action: please click on the header of this box to see the available options. #> 8 By default, the points (cells) are not colored.

Points can be displayed using violin plots stratified by an experimental factor on the x-axis, or as a scatter plot involving continuous variables on both the x- and y-axes. #> 12 The plotting behaviour will also change depending on the type of data being plotted. This is best illustrated with Column data plot 1.

Action: click on the header of this collapsible box. #> 13 Currently, there is only one violin plot.

Action: click on Column data. #> 14 You can see how this now changes to a scatter plot when plotting two continuous variables against each other. #> 15 Action: click on (or type) driver_1_s. #> 16 The plot now changes to a grouped violin plot for a categorical variable on the x-axis. Note that a horizontal violin plot can also be generated if the categorical variable is assigned to the y-axis. #> 17 Action: click on (or type) dissection_s. #> 18 The plot now changes to a Hinton plot for two categorical variables. The size of each rectangle corresponds to the number of points in each combination of covariate levels. #> 19 A Feature assay plot displays the assay values for a chosen feature (here, gene expression) across all cells. Like the Column data plot, points represent cells and can be shown in both violin or scatter plots, depending on the variable selected on the x-axis. #> 20 A Column data table displays the contents of the colData of your input object as a table. #> 21 Similarly, a Row data table displays the contents of the rowData of your input object as a table. #> 22 You can also plot the rowData values against each other with a Row data plot. #> 23 A Sample assay plot displays the assay values across features for a chosen sample on the y-axis (possibly against another sample on the x-axis). This is best used for bulk datasets where it is more feasible to inspect individual samples. #> 24 You can produce a Complex heat map to visualize a feature-by-sample matrix of assay values, for a selected subset of features. #> 25 The Selection parameters box contains parameters to handle sharing of multiple point selections across panels. The idea is that points selected in a "transmitting" panel can be visualized in a "receiving" panel.

In this manner, we can construct arbitrarily complex (non-circular) networks between panels to display only a subset of points that match a certain criteria. This is equivalent to multi-step gating schemes in flow cytometry, provided the selection effect is set to Restrict.

Another important thing to keep in mind when selecting points from violin plots is that points will be selected only if the brushed area includes the center of the x-tick, i.e., the center of the violin plot.
